source.text: The Ten Vast Practices and Vows from the chapter on Samantabhadra's Practices and Vows, Avataṃsaka Sutra, fascicle 40
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

b01.heading: The Ten Great Practices and Vows
b01.plain: Then Samantabhadra Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having praised the Tathāgata's surpassing merits, said to the bodhisattvas and to Sudhana: "Good son, even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions went on describing the Tathāgata's merits for as many kalpas as there are motes of dust in unspeakably many Buddha-lands, they could not exhaust them. Whoever wishes to enter this gate of merit should cultivate ten vast practices and vows. What are the ten? First, to pay homage and respect to all Buddhas; second, to praise the Tathāgatas; third, to make offerings widely; fourth, to repent of karmic obstacles; fifth, to rejoice in others' merit; sixth, to request the Buddhas to turn the Dharma wheel; seventh, to request the Buddhas to remain in the world; eighth, always to follow the Buddhas in learning; ninth, always to accord with beings; tenth, to dedicate all merit universally."
b01.commentary: This is the final chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sutra: the teaching Sudhana hears from Samantabhadra at the end of his pilgrimage to fifty-three spiritual friends. These ten vows are regarded as the practical charter of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path and are often chanted at services and Dharma gatherings.

b02.heading: First, Paying Homage to All Buddhas
b02.plain: Good son, paying homage to all Buddhas means this. Throughout the whole Dharma realm and the realm of space, there are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as many as the motes of dust in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and three times. By the power of Samantabhadra's practices and vows, I give rise to deep faith and understanding, as if they were before my eyes, and with pure body, speech and mind I always pay them homage. Before each Buddha I manifest unspeakably many bodies, and each body bows to unspeakably many Buddhas. When the realm of space comes to an end, my homage will end; but since the realm of space can never end, this homage of mine is endless. In the same way, when the realm of beings, the karma of beings and the afflictions of beings come to an end, my homage will end; but since they never end, this homage of mine is endless. It continues thought after thought without a break, and body, speech and mind never tire of it.
b02.commentary: The refrain "when the realm of space ends, my vow will end" repeats in every one of the ten vows. Since space and beings are endless, the vow is endless too: this line symbolizes the infinite resolve of Samantabhadra's vows.

b03.heading: Second, Praising the Tathāgatas
b03.plain: Praising the Tathāgatas means this. Throughout the whole Dharma realm and the realm of space, in every finest mote of dust in all the lands of the ten directions and three times, there are as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust in all worlds, and each Buddha is surrounded by an ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas. With deep and excellent understanding, knowing them as if before my eyes, with subtle tongues surpassing the goddess of eloquence, each tongue sending forth an endless ocean of sounds and each sound an ocean of words, I extol and praise the ocean of merit of all the Tathāgatas, continuing without a break to the end of the future, reaching everywhere throughout the Dharma realm.
b03.commentary: Countless Buddhas within a single mote of dust shows the Avataṃsaka worldview that "in one is all."

b04.heading: Third, Making Offerings Widely
b04.plain: Making offerings widely means this. In every mote of dust in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and three times, throughout the whole Dharma realm and the realm of space, there are as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust in all worlds, each surrounded by an ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas. By the power of Samantabhadra's practices and vows, I give rise to deep faith and understanding and, knowing them as if before my eyes, I make offerings with the finest of all offerings. … Good son, among all offerings, the offering of Dharma is supreme: the offering of practicing as taught, the offering of benefiting beings, the offering of embracing beings, the offering of taking on the suffering of beings, the offering of diligently cultivating roots of goodness, the offering of never abandoning the bodhisattva's work, and the offering of never parting from the mind of awakening.
b04.commentary: The key point is that the offering of Dharma, living by the teaching and helping beings, surpasses offerings of flowers and incense.

b05.heading: Fourth, Repenting of Karmic Obstacles
b05.plain: Repenting of karmic obstacles means this. The bodhisattva reflects: "Through beginningless kalpas past, because of greed, anger and delusion, I have done measureless, boundless harmful deeds with body, speech and mind. If this harmful karma had a form, all of space could not hold it. Now, with pure body, speech and mind, before all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in worlds as many as motes of dust throughout the Dharma realm, I sincerely repent, will not do it again, and will always abide in the pure precepts and all merit."
b05.commentary: This is the same spirit as the repentance verse of the Thousand Hands Sutra, "All the harmful karma I have created in the past." Repentance does not stop at regretting the past; it goes on to the resolve never to repeat it.

b06.heading: Fifth, Rejoicing in Merit
b06.plain: Rejoicing in merit means this. All the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as many as the motes of dust throughout the whole Dharma realm and the realm of space in the ten directions and three times, from the time they first aroused the mind, diligently cultivated merit for the sake of all-knowing wisdom, not sparing body or life, through unspeakably many kalpas … they practiced every hard austerity, perfected the many pāramitās, entered the many stages of bodhisattva wisdom, attained supreme awakening, entered nirvana and distributed their relics. In all these roots of goodness I rejoice. And in all the merit of every kind of being in all the worlds of the ten directions, in the six destinies and the four kinds of birth, even merit as small as a mote of dust, I rejoice.
b06.commentary: This teaches that simply rejoicing in others' good deeds as if they were one's own, without envy, is itself great merit. Everything from the Buddhas' merit to the good deeds of the smallest creature becomes cause for rejoicing.

b07.heading: Sixth, Requesting the Dharma Wheel Be Turned
b07.plain: Requesting the turning of the Dharma wheel means this. In every mote of dust in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and three times, throughout the whole Dharma realm and the realm of space, there are unspeakably many vast Buddha-lands. In each land, thought after thought, unspeakably many Buddhas attain right awakening, surrounded by ocean-like assemblies of bodhisattvas. With body, speech and mind, by every skillful means, I earnestly request them to turn the wondrous Dharma wheel.
b07.commentary: To turn the Dharma wheel means to spread the teaching. This vow comes from the story of the god Brahmā, who begged the newly awakened Buddha to teach.

b08.heading: Seventh, Requesting the Buddhas to Remain in the World
b08.plain: Requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world means this. To all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as many as the motes of dust throughout the Dharma realm and the realm of space in the ten directions and three times, who are about to enter nirvana, and to all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, those still learning and those beyond learning, and to all good spiritual friends, I make this request: do not enter nirvana, but remain for as many kalpas as there are motes of dust in all Buddha-lands, to benefit and gladden all beings.
b08.commentary: This is the wish that good teachers stay with us long. Notice that the request is made not only to the Buddhas but to all good spiritual friends.

b09.heading: Eighth, Always Following the Buddhas in Learning
b09.plain: Always following the Buddhas in learning means this. Vairocana Tathāgata of this Sahā world, from the time he first aroused the mind, strove without retreating and gave away unspeakably many bodies and lives. Peeling off his skin for paper, splitting his bones for brushes and drawing his blood for ink, he copied sutras until they piled as high as Mount Sumeru. Because he valued the Dharma, he did not spare even body and life, let alone throne, cities, villages, palaces, gardens and all his possessions. All his other hard practices, his attaining great awakening beneath the tree, his displays of spiritual powers and transformations, his appearing in many Buddha-bodies among many assemblies … up to his showing entry into nirvana: all of this I follow and learn.
b09.commentary: "Skin for paper, bones for brushes, blood for ink" is a famous image of how deeply he valued the Dharma, and it became the spirit of the practice of copying sutras.

b10.heading: Ninth, Always According with Beings
b10.plain: Always according with beings means this. The beings in all the ocean of worlds of the ten directions, throughout the Dharma realm and the realm of space, differ in countless ways … I accord with them all, serving them in many ways and making offerings in many ways, as I would honor my parents, serve my teachers and elders, or attend arhats and Tathāgatas, without any difference. To the sick I become a good doctor; to those who have lost their way I show the right road; in the dark of night I become a light; to the poor I reveal hidden treasure. In this way the bodhisattva benefits all beings equally. Why? If a bodhisattva accords with beings, that is according with and making offerings to the Buddhas; if they respect and serve beings, that is respecting and serving the Tathāgatas; if they make beings happy, that makes all the Tathāgatas happy. … Therefore awakening belongs to beings. Without beings, no bodhisattva could ever attain supreme, right awakening.
b10.commentary: "Awakening belongs to beings" is the most famous line of this chapter. It is followed by a parable likening beings to the roots of a great tree and the Buddhas to its flowers and fruit.

b11.heading: Tenth, Dedicating All Merit Universally
b11.plain: Dedicating merit universally means this. All the merit from the first homage up to according with beings I dedicate entirely to all beings throughout the Dharma realm and the realm of space. May beings always be at peace and happy, free of sickness and pain; may every harmful act they try to do fail, and every good deed they cultivate quickly succeed; may the gates of all evil realms be shut and the right road to humans, heavens and nirvana be opened. If beings are to receive the heaviest painful results of the harmful karma they have piled up, I will take them all on in their place, so that those beings may all be freed and finally attain supreme awakening.
b11.commentary: Dedication means not using the merit gathered through the nine vows for oneself, but turning it to all beings. The bodhisattva's compassion reaches its height in the vow to bear beings' suffering in their place.

samantabhadra.definition: The bodhisattva of practice and vows. Together with Mañjuśrī, bodhisattva of wisdom, he attends Śākyamuni Buddha.

sudhana.definition: The seeker in the Entering the Dharma Realm chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sutra who visits fifty-three spiritual friends in search of awakening.

dharmadhatu.definition: The whole world in which all things and phenomena unfold. In the Avataṃsaka Sutra, a world where everything blends together without obstruction.

three-poisons.definition: Greed, anger and delusion: the three poisons at the root of all afflictions.

dharmacakra.definition: The Buddha's teaching likened to a wheel: the teaching rolls far and wide, crushing afflictions.

vairocana.definition: The Dharma-body Buddha whose body is truth itself; the principal Buddha of the Avataṃsaka Sutra.

parinamana.definition: Turning the merit one has cultivated toward other beings or toward awakening.
